extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two main conformity assessment procedures for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometric systems), the provider may choose between the internal control procedure or a notified-body assessment, depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies additionally verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements.

Annex VII (notified body) assessment is described by industry sources as mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical-infrastructure AI, while most other high-risk systems may use the Annex VI self-assessment route.

Providers may choose any notified body for the conformity assessment procedure, except that where the high-risk AI system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions/bodies, the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body instead.
A new conformity assessment is required if a high-risk AI system is substantially modified, except for predetermined changes in systems that continue to learn after being placed on the market.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority to derogate from the standard conformity assessment procedure and authorise placing a specific high-risk AI system on the market, for a limited time, for exceptional reasons of public security, health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial/infrastructural assets.

Under Annex VII point 4.5, a notified body may, after exhausting other reasonable means and upon reasoned request, be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, including relevant parameters, when necessary to assess conformity with Chapter III Section 2 requirements.

The Commission maintains the NANDO (New Approach Notified and Designated Organisations) database/system as the register of designated notified bodies across EU product legislation, including medical devices regulations.
As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 notified bodies designated under the Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and 19 under the In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR); these are not AI Act designations.

A Council document (ST-7322-2026) sets out a coding system (AIA codes, e.g., AIP 0101 etc.) that defines the scope of designation of conformity assessment bodies notified under Article 30 of the referenced regulation, corresponding to Annex I categories of the AI Act.

A Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) proposes creating a new Annex XIV to integrate AI Act high-risk categories into the NANDO information system and to amend Regulation (EU) 2018/1139 for smooth integration of AI Act requirements; as of its text this is a proposal for a Regulation, not yet adopted law.

As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem for the AI Act was still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and limited capacity ahead of the August 2026 deadline for high-risk AI obligations.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act in the medical devices/SaMD context.

High-risk AI obligations under the AI Act are stated to fully apply from August 2026, after which notified bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments.

A news source discussing the separate Cyber Resilience Act (CRA, not the AI Act) states that as of late June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated for the CRA, with a target of sufficient notified body capacity by 11 December 2026 and full application of the CRA from 11 December 2027.
The 2022 proposal version of Article 43 differs in structure/wording from the final adopted text of Article 43 in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

contradictions.claim_a: No notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act as of March/April 2026, according to industry blog sources.
contradictions.claim_b: No official EU source (eu_guidance or official_eu) among those provided confirms or denies a specific designation count for AI Act notified bodies; only MDR/IVDR designation counts are confirmed via NANDO as of October 2025.
contradictions.description: Sources 21 and 22 (industry blogs, no official citation) assert zero AI Act notified body designations as of early-mid 2026, while the only official NANDO data available (source 7) pertains to MDR/IVDR designations, not the AI Act, leaving the actual current AI Act designation status unverified by an authoritative source.

contradictions.claim_b: This is sometimes conflated in secondary commentary with AI Act notified body timelines, but the CRA (Cyber Resilience Act) is a distinct regulation from the AI Act with its own notified body regime and deadlines (June 2026 application, December 2027 full application).
contradictions.description: Source 20 covers the Cyber Resilience Act's notified body regime and deadlines, which are distinct from the AI Act's notified body regime discussed in source 23; readers could mistakenly conflate the two regulations' timelines and designation statuses.

open_issues: No official EU source in this set (eu_guidance or official_eu) confirms a specific count or list of notified bodies formally designated under the AI Act itself, as opposed to under MDR/IVDR or other sectoral regimes.

The exact adoption status and timeline of the proposed new Annex XIV / NANDO integration regulation (COM(2025) 836) is unclear — it is referenced only as a proposal moving through the Council (source 9) without confirmation of final adoption or entry into force.

The precise relationship and cross-references between the Council coding document (source 8) and the final adopted Article 30/35 designation framework of the AI Act are not fully detailed in the sources.

It is unclear from the sources whether, by the current date (October 2026), any notified bodies have in fact been designated under the AI Act, given the August 2026 deadline for high-risk obligations and conflicting industry reports from March-April 2026 claiming none had been designated at that time.

One source (15) asserts an 'algorithm passport' registration requirement with the AI Office as a legal requirement, but no other source (including official AI Act Service Desk articles on Article 43 and related provisions) supports or mentions such a requirement; this claim appears unsupported and should not be treated as an actual legal requirement.

The sources do not clarify how the Article 46 derogation procedure interacts in practice with notified body assessments once notified bodies become available, nor how many such derogations have been granted to date.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two primary conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems under Article 43: internal control (Annex VI) or notified-body assessment (Annex VII), with the applicable route depending on the system's Annex III category or its link to existing sectoral product legislation (high confidence). However, the actual notified-body ecosystem for the AI Act remains largely unverified by official sources, with only conflicting industry reports suggesting that, as of early-to-mid 2026, few or no bodies had been formally designated under the Act itself, distinct from the well-established NANDO registrations under medical devices legislation.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act sets out two main pathways for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [FPF Conformity Assessment Guide](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For high-risk systems already covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Annex I Section A, providers must follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). For biometric systems under Annex III point 1, providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, though this claim rests on lower-confidence, partly outdated sourcing (low confidence) ([Futurium EU AI Approach](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf); [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). Industry commentary suggests that notified-body assessment is effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems may rely on self-assessment, though this interpretation carries low confidence ([Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment); [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

Providers generally may choose any notified body, except where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority performs this role instead (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 43, GA](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). A new conformity assessment is required for substantial modifications, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard procedures and authorise market placement for limited periods on public security, health, or environmental grounds (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 46](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, as a last resort and upon reasoned request, gain access to training and trained models and relevant parameters to assess compliance (medium confidence) ([Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
The Commission maintains NANDO as the EU-wide register of designated notified bodies across product legislation, including medical devices regulation (high confidence) ([NANDO/MDR consolidated text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02017R0745-20260101); [DG SANTE](https://health.ec.europa.eu/medical-devices-topics-interest/notified-bodies-medical-devices_en)). As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 bodies under MDR and 19 under IVDR—these figures relate to medical devices, not the AI Act (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex evaluation document](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). A Council document (ST-7322-2026) sets out an AIA coding system defining designation scope for conformity assessment bodies corresponding to Annex I categories (medium confidence) ([Council ST-7322-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)), and a Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would create a new Annex XIV integrating AI Act categories into NANDO, though this remains an unadopted proposal (medium confidence) ([Council ST-15708-2025](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

Several low-confidence industry sources report that, as of March–April 2026, the AI Act notified-body ecosystem was still being built with no formal designations confirmed, ahead of the August 2026 high-risk obligations deadline ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act); [AIAct Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide); [MDX CRO](https://mdxcro.com/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-samd)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
No official EU source confirms the current count or identity of notified bodies designated specifically under the AI Act, as distinct from MDR/IVDR. Industry blog claims of "zero designations" (low confidence, below 0.4) conflict with the absence of any authoritative counter-evidence, leaving the true status unverified. A separate source on the Cyber Resilience Act's notified-body timeline risks being conflated with the AI Act's regime but addresses a distinct instrument (low confidence) ([CyberCertLabs](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)). The 2022 proposal text of Article 43 differs from the final adopted version, so older sources referencing the proposal should not be treated as current law (high confidence) ([2022 Proposal Text](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html)).

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether any notified bodies have been formally designated under the AI Act as of late 2026, given the August 2026 deadline. The adoption status and timeline of the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration regulation is unconfirmed. The interaction between Article 46 derogations and notified-body assessments in practice, and how many derogations have been granted, is not documented in available sources. One source claims an "algorithm passport" registration requirement with the AI Office as a legal obligation, but no official source (including the AI Act Service Desk's articles on Article 43 and related provisions) corroborates such a requirement; readers should treat this as an unverified, unsupported claim rather than an actual legal requirement. Finally, the precise relationship between the Council's AIA coding document (ST-7322-2026) and the final adopted Article 30/35 designation framework is not fully detailed in the available sources, leaving open how the proposed coding scheme maps onto the Act's legally binding designation provisions.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two primary conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems under Article 43: internal control (Annex VI) or notified-body assessment (Annex VII), with the applicable route depending on the system's Annex III category or its link to existing sectoral product legislation (high confidence). However, the actual notified-body ecosystem for the AI Act remains largely unverified by official sources, with only conflicting industry reports suggesting that, as of early-to-mid 2026, few or no bodies had been formally designated under the Act itself, distinct from the well-established NANDO registrations under medical devices legislation.

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act sets out two main pathways for high-risk AI systems: internal control based on Annex VI, or assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation by a notified body based on Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [FPF Conformity Assessment Guide](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For high-risk systems already covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Annex I Section A, providers must follow that sectoral legislation's conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies additionally verifying AI-specific requirements (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). For biometric systems under Annex III point 1, providers may choose between internal control or notified-body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied, though this claim rests on lower-confidence, partly outdated sourcing (low confidence) ([Futurium EU AI Approach](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf); [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). Industry commentary suggests that notified-body assessment is effectively mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical-infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems may rely on self-assessment, though this interpretation carries low confidence ([Quantamix Solutions](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment); [Openlayer](https://www.openlayer.com/blog/eu-ai-act-compliance-checklist-high-risk-systems)).

Providers generally may choose any notified body, except where the system is intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority performs this role instead (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 43, GA](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). A new conformity assessment is required for substantial modifications, except for predetermined changes in continuously learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 43](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard procedures and authorise market placement for limited periods on public security, health, or environmental grounds (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Article 46](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)). Under Annex VII point 4.5, notified bodies may, as a last resort and upon reasoned request, gain access to training and trained models and relevant parameters to assess compliance (medium confidence) ([Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
The Commission maintains NANDO as the EU-wide register of designated notified bodies across product legislation, including medical devices regulation (high confidence) ([NANDO/MDR consolidated text](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02017R0745-20260101); [DG SANTE](https://health.ec.europa.eu/medical-devices-topics-interest/notified-bodies-medical-devices_en)). As of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 bodies under MDR and 19 under IVDR—these figures relate to medical devices, not the AI Act (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex evaluation document](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). A Council document (ST-7322-2026) sets out an AIA coding system defining designation scope for conformity assessment bodies corresponding to Annex I categories (medium confidence) ([Council ST-7322-2026](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)), and a Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would create a new Annex XIV integrating AI Act categories into NANDO, though this remains an unadopted proposal (medium confidence) ([Council ST-15708-2025](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

Several low-confidence industry sources report that, as of March–April 2026, the AI Act notified-body ecosystem was still being built with no formal designations confirmed, ahead of the August 2026 high-risk obligations deadline ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act); [AIAct Navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide); [MDX CRO](https://mdxcro.com/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-samd)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
No official EU source confirms the current count or identity of notified bodies designated specifically under the AI Act, as distinct from MDR/IVDR. Industry blog claims of "zero designations" (low confidence, below 0.4) conflict with the absence of any authoritative counter-evidence, leaving the true status unverified. A separate source on the Cyber Resilience Act's notified-body timeline risks being conflated with the AI Act's regime but addresses a distinct instrument (low confidence) ([CyberCertLabs](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)). The 2022 proposal text of Article 43 differs from the final adopted version, so older sources referencing the proposal should not be treated as current law (high confidence) ([2022 Proposal Text](https://www.artificial-intelligence-act.com/Artificial_Intelligence_Act_Article_43_(Proposal_25.11.2022).html)).

## Knowledge Gaps
It remains unclear whether any notified bodies have been formally designated under the AI Act as of late 2026, given the August 2026 deadline. The adoption status and timeline of the proposed Annex XIV/NANDO integration regulation is unconfirmed. The interaction between Article 46 derogations and notified-body assessments in practice, and how many derogations have been granted, is not documented in available sources.
